name: Dip bars

lead: Dip bars, or dip stations, are two horizontal handles at about hip height or higher. The user supports their bodyweight on straight arms, lowers and presses back up. It is a home-friendly way to fill out the lower chest, front shoulders and triceps, and it pairs with pull-ups for balanced pressing and pulling.

Pressing away from the handles loads the pectorals, triceps and front deltoids, and a forward lean shifts more work to the chest. Dips can be progressed with weight belts or vests, slower reps and pauses. Dip-specific research is sparse; proponents rely on general resistance-training findings that muscle grows across a wide range of loads taken near failure.

paras: Users add dips to upper-body days, aiming for steady increases in reps and then added weight. Stands come freestanding, wall-mounted or as power-rack attachments.

Deep dips place the shoulder in extension and internal rotation, a known irritant for people with shoulder problems, and elbow tendon strain is reported. Unstable or narrow low-cost stands are a safety issue.

angle.text: Users do dips on parallel bars to build the chest, shoulders and triceps with bodyweight, filling out the upper body at home. Bodyweight resistance training is studied for muscle growth; dips themselves are mostly discussed in coaching sources.

lead: Dip bars, also called parallel bars or dip stations, are a pair of horizontal handles set at about hip height or higher. The user grips them with arms extended, lowers the body by bending the elbows until the shoulders are slightly below the elbows, and presses back up [1]. They are sold as freestanding stands, wall-mounted bars, attachments for power racks and small portable units.

The dip is a compound bodyweight pressing exercise that mainly loads the triceps, with the chest (pectoralis major) and the front of the shoulder (anterior deltoid) also involved [1]. An upright torso is described as shifting emphasis to the triceps and a forward lean as shifting it to the chest and shoulders [1]. In looksmaxxing discussion, dip bars are associated with building upper-body mass, particularly the lower chest, shoulders and triceps, using only bodyweight and optionally added load.

No published trials appear to have tested dip bars as a product, and dip-specific research is sparse. General resistance-training meta-analyses show muscle growth across a wide range of loads taken near failure [2], which is the evidence base proponents typically rely on.

paras: In a standard dip the lifter supports the body on straight arms, lowers under control and pushes back up to lockout [1]. Technique guidance in the source material advises keeping the shoulders retracted and depressed and controlling the descent to limit excessive shoulder extension [1]. Dips can be made easier with bands, machines or benches, and harder by hanging load from a dip belt [1].

The apparatus ranges from basic two-post stands to heavy-duty rack-integrated bars. Stability, handle width and handle height are the features that most affect how well a station suits the exercise, and cheaper narrow stands are sometimes criticised in hobbyist forums for wobble. Gymnastics forums discuss parallel bars with a focus on rigidity and adjustable width.

According to one machine-written encyclopedia entry, the parallel bars were developed by the German educator Friedrich Ludwig Jahn in the 1810s as part of the Turnen gymnastics system, and dip-type exercises later featured in European and United States military physical training [1]. The same source says the exercise became a staple of bodybuilding in the 1950s and 1960s, citing Vince Gironda's wide-grip variation, and that Jack LaLanne promoted dips on television [1]. These claims come from a single non-human-edited source and are not independently verified here.

Direct research on dips is limited. The source material describes electromyographic work ranking dips highly for triceps activation, and the American Council on Exercise is cited as including them among top triceps exercises [1]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of low-load versus high-load resistance training reports hypertrophy and strength adaptations across loading ranges, which applies to any progressively loaded exercise rather than to dips alone [2].

Deep dips place the shoulder in extension under body weight. Sources describe improper form as potentially causing anterior shoulder impingement and increased shear forces at the joint, and say the exercise may be unsuitable for people with existing shoulder or elbow problems without modification [1]. Elbow tendon strain is also commonly reported anecdotally. Unstable stands are a separate equipment-related hazard.
No studies found. Research on resistance training in general, including meta-analyses of loading, exists [2], but no clinical trial has examined dip bars or dips for appearance outcomes.

Dip bars are discussed as a low-cost way to add pressing volume at home, often paired with pull-ups for balanced upper-body training. Threads on strength and gymnastics forums focus on station stability and bar dimensions. Community material specific to appearance claims is limited.

timeline.event: Friedrich Ludwig Jahn is credited in one source with developing the parallel bars within the Turnen gymnastics system [1].
Dips are reported to become a core bodybuilding exercise, with Jack LaLanne promoting them on television [1].
